study_identification.author_journal_year: Kim et al., Nature Mental Health, 2024
study_identification.title: Mapping cerebellar anatomical heterogeneity in mental and neurological illnesses

study_characteristics.study_objective: To map the normative development and aging of the cerebellum across the lifespan at voxel-wise spatial precision using >54,000 participants, and to reveal heterogeneity within five clinical illnesses (ASD, MCI, AD, BD, and SZ) by applying normative models to quantify individual-level deviations from population norms.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The normative model addresses some aspects of nuisance structure but not all comprehensively. Site effects are handled by including scanning site as a fixed effect. The Bayesian linear regression with likelihood warping using 'sinarcsinsh' transformation is designed to handle non-Gaussian predictive distributions and correct for outer centiles, addressing distributional shape issues. Quality control procedures excluded outliers (>5 SD imputed by mean). However, the paper does not explicitly discuss handling of other nuisance structures such as within-site variance heterogeneity, family/sibling structure, or longitudinal correlations (only baseline scans used). Site-specific variance modeling appears limited to fixed effects rather than hierarchical variance structure. The matched sensitivity analyses (Supplementary) suggest awareness of confounding but were conducted post-hoc rather than incorporated into the primary model.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Methods: 'We employed a Bayesian linear regression with likelihood warping approach, specifically using the 'sinarcsinsh' transformation. This approach is well suited for handling nonlinear basis functions and non-Gaussian predictive distributions for large datasets as well as correcting for outer centiles.' 'To account for scanner effects, we treated the scanning site as a fixed effect in our analysis.' 'Results that deviated more than five standards of deviation were imputed by the mean.' Supplementary Methods: 'For supplementary analyses, we conducted statistical comparisons between clinical cohorts and their sex-, age-, and scanning-site-matched groups.'

'To determine participants with extreme deviations, we set a threshold at z > |1.96|, corresponding to the 95% confidence interval. For example, deviations with z scores greater than 1.96 were identified as extreme positive deviations, indicating significantly increased volume compared with the control pattern and vice versa for extreme negative deviations.' Atlas-based analyses: 'By mapping the deviations onto specific anatomical regions... We separately calculated the percentage of extreme positive and negative deviations for each participant in the regions of interest in reference to the existing atlases. We divided this by the size of the region and multiplied the resulting proportion by 100 (deriving a percentage of extreme positive or negative deviations per region).'

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons; Rank biserial correlation for effect sizes; Spearman correlation analyses between percentage of extreme deviations and cognitive/symptom scores (FIQ, VIQ, PIQ, ADOS, PANSS); Analyses conducted separately for anatomical atlas (28 lobules), task-based atlas (10 regions), and resting-state atlas (17 networks); Multiple comparison correction accounting for number of tests, regions of interest, and directions (positive/negative); Only correlations with corrected P < 0.05 considered statistically significant
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Cerebellar morphology shows substantial individual heterogeneity within all five clinical illnesses, with ASD and MCI exhibiting increased bidirectional extreme deviations, while SZ and AD show predominantly negative deviations; extreme deviations are associated with cognitive scores in ASD and SZ.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The study established voxel-wise cerebellar normative models across the lifespan (age 3-85) from >54,000 individuals across 132 sites. Group-level analyses revealed significant negative deviations (lower cerebellar volumes) in SZ patients, particularly in posterior regions, consistent with previous reports. AD showed significant reductions in lobular measures (especially right crus I) but voxel-wise effects did not survive multiple comparison correction. ASD exhibited small negative effects in posterior regions and medium effects in regions related to action observation and dorsal attention network. MCI and ASD groups showed significant small effects in both positive and negative deviations, suggesting possible compensatory mechanisms in some individuals. Individual-level normative probability maps revealed high heterogeneity within diagnostic groups, with only marginal percentages of individuals showing extreme deviations in the same regions. Association analyses found that in ASD, regions in right IV-VI and somatomotor B network showed positive correlations between percentage of extreme positive deviations and estimated PIQ (survived correction). In SZ, participants with extreme positive deviations showed positive correlation with estimated full-scale IQ, while those with extreme negative deviations showed negative correlation with IQ. Symptom scores (ADOS for ASD, PANSS for SZ) did not show significant associations after multiple comparison correction. Matched control analyses yielded similar but statistically weaker effects than full-sample analyses. The results demonstrate the cerebellum's nuanced role across different mental and neurological illnesses and highlight the importance of individual-level precision medicine approaches.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Lack of coherent behavioral, cognitive, genetic, and medical history information across combined datasets; Relatively low coverage in very young ages and 30-40 age range; Primarily represents Western European populations, limiting generalizability to other ethnicities; Cross-sectional data limits examination of drug/treatment effects; Incomplete medication information in TOP study; Inferior cerebellar regions may have poorer model fits due to imaging challenges; Cerebellar topography shows substantial individual differences that may not align with average atlases, limiting functional interpretation; IQ estimates based on wide range of tests across groups rather than standardized measures; Correlation does not imply causation regarding cerebellar deviations and cognitive function
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The models are made publicly available via PCNportal (https://pcnportal.dccn.nl/) for use by other researchers. The voxel-wise approach allows integration with any existing or future cerebellar atlas morphed into MNI space, providing flexibility for diverse research questions. The paper demonstrates application to three different atlases (anatomical, task-based, resting-state) to enhance interpretability of deviations. Future applications could include dividing heterogeneous clinical populations into subtypes based on deviation patterns, enhancing biomarker development using comprehensive cognitive and behavioral measures, and incorporating longitudinal datasets to track individual trajectories over time.

general_notes.general_notes: This is one of the largest cerebellar normative modeling studies to date with >54,000 participants. The study provides approximately 143,000 normative models (voxel-wise plus lobular). Data and models are shared openly via PCNportal. Supplementary materials include extensive sensitivity analyses including matched case-control analyses, ethnicity comparisons (European subset), ASD subgroup analyses (Asperger's vs Autism), and medication effects in SZ. The study used state-of-the-art preprocessing including ACAPULCO algorithm for cerebellar parcellation and SUIT toolbox for voxel-based morphometry. Quality control was comprehensive using ENIGMA Cerebellum Volumetric Pipeline. The paper demonstrates the value of normative modeling for capturing individual-level heterogeneity that is obscured in traditional group-level analyses. Published online August 22, 2024, in Nature Mental Health.
